extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of poetry; literary critics and those learning to judge poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging, appreciating, and selecting 'the best' poetry: how to form a sound critical estimate, what pitfalls to avoid (historic/personal bias), and which formal and substantive qualities to look for in great poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inviolableness against charlatanism
rubrics_metrics.description: "In poetry, which is thought and art in one, it is the glory, the eternal honor, that charlatanism shall find no entrance; that this noble sphere be kept inviolate and inviolable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charlatanism is any confusion or obliteration of the distinctions between excellent and inferior, sound and unsound, true and untrue. It is impermissible in poetry because it obscures the difference between what is of real poetic value and what is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for the real estimate (seek the best)
rubrics_metrics.description: We should set before our minds a sense for the best, the really excellent, and let that govern our estimate of what we read: "A clearer, deeper sense of the best is the most precious benefit which we can gather from a poetical collection."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constantly revert to the desire to feel and enjoy the truly excellent; make the pursuit of the best the guiding principle in studying poets and poetry (cum multa legeris... ad unum semper oportet redire principium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the historic estimate fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The historic estimate mistakes a poet's value as a stage in national or linguistic development for his intrinsic poetic merit: "A poet or a poem may count to us historically... they may count to us historically."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-rate works merely because of their place in literary history or because they illuminate origins; historic importance can lead critics to exaggerate poetic quality (examples: over-praising early French romance-poetry or equating Cædmon with Milton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the personal estimate fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal affinities, likings, and circumstances can make us attach more importance to a poet's work than it really possesses: "Our personal affinities... have great power to sway our estimate..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be watchful that private significance or personal taste does not cause exaggerated praise; distinguish what counts 'to us' personally from what counts 'really' as poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use masterly passages as touchstones
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep always in mind lines and expressions of the great masters as a touchstone: "there can be no more useful help... than to have always in one's mind lines and expressions of the great masters, and to apply them as a touchstone to other poetry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorize short passages or single lines from Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, Milton, etc.; concrete examples are more instructive than abstract lists of qualities and help detect presence or absence of high poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance/matter criterion: poetic truth and seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The substance and matter of the best poetry acquire their special character from possessing, in an eminent degree, truth and seriousness (following Aristotle: poetry has a higher truth and higher seriousness than history).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the 'matter' of a poem by how much it conveys deep truth and an earnest seriousness; such qualities give poetry its superior critical power over life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style/manner criterion: diction and movement
rubrics_metrics.description: The style and manner of the best poetry are given their special character by diction and, even more, by movement: "to the style and manner of the best poetry their special character, their accent, is given by their diction, and, even yet more, by their movement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to word-choice (diction) and the rhythmic/musical flow (movement) of verse; excellence in these marks high poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of substance and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: The superiority of substance (truth and seriousness) is inseparable from the superiority of diction and movement: "The two superiorities are closely related, and are in steadfast proportion one to the other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that where high poetic truth and seriousness are lacking, the corresponding excellence in diction and movement will also be absent; assess both together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concrete application to abstract definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete examples of masters' verse teach poetic quality far better than abstract prose descriptions: "They are far better recognized by being felt in the verse of the master, than by being perused in the prose of the critic."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asked to define poetic excellence, rely primarily on showing exemplary passages and applying general principles to actual poems rather than producing abstract lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware excessive philological/historical scholarship distracting enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: Elaborate philological groundwork may be an admirable theoretical preparation but in practice it often distracts from enjoyment and leads to overrating less-good works: (schoolboys' Greek/Latin study analogy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical investigation should serve the end of deeper enjoyment of the truly excellent; avoid letting research substitute for the direct appreciation of masterpieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain open-eyed appreciation of classics
rubrics_metrics.description: Read classics with 'open eyes' and not with 'eyes blinded with superstition'—perceive when a classic comes short and rate it properly: "True, we must read our classic with open eyes..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While enjoying a real classic deeply, still acknowledge defects; use negative criticism only insofar as it leads to clearer enjoyment of the best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for classic status: sustained high seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a 'real classic' the work must belong to the class of the very best, and possess the 'high and excellent seriousness' (spoudaiotēs) that marks the greatest poets; lacking this, a poet (e.g., Chaucer) may be excellent but not a great classic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poet's seriousness (a sustained, elevated criticism of life) is present; absence means the work cannot be elevated to the highest class despite other virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize period/mission limits on poetic virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic virtues may be limited by historical missions of an age: e.g., the eighteenth century's emphasis on regularity, uniformity, precision, balance (qualities of 'a fit prose') served a national prose mission but repressed imaginative poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the cultural and historical functions that shaped poetic style—distinguish virtues appropriate to an age's mission from universal poetic excellence; this helps avoid misplacing classic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of poetry as criticism of life depends on excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: The criticism of life which poetry offers will be of power in proportion as the poetry conveying it is excellent rather than inferior, sound rather than unsound, true rather than untrue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how effectively a poem performs as a 'criticism of life'—its consolatory and formative power correlates with its intrinsic poetic excellence.
